subject: Physics
central_question: How did scattering and atomic spectra lead from early atomic models to Bohr’s quantised description of the hydrogen atom?
in_scope_units: Introduction to Thomson’s model, characteristic atomic spectra and the need to understand atomic structure.
Geiger–Marsden alpha-particle scattering experiment and Rutherford’s nuclear model.
Observed scattering distribution, the small dense nucleus and the largely empty atom.
Alpha-particle trajectory, impact parameter, scattering angle and distance of closest approach.
Electron orbits in the Rutherford model, Coulomb attraction, kinetic energy, potential energy and negative total energy.
Atomic emission and absorption line spectra as element-specific fingerprints.
Instability and continuous-spectrum predictions of the classical Rutherford atom.
Bohr’s three postulates for stationary states, angular-momentum quantisation and radiative transitions.
Allowed radii and quantised energies of hydrogen stationary states.
Ground state, excited states, ionisation energy and the hydrogen energy-level diagram.
Hydrogen line spectrum produced by transitions between discrete energy levels.
de Broglie standing-wave explanation of Bohr’s angular-momentum condition.
Successes and limitations of Bohr’s model for hydrogenic and multi-electron atoms.
banned_topics: Detailed nuclear composition, mass defect, radioactivity, fission and fusion, which belong to Chapter 13: Nuclei.
Detailed photoelectric effect and photon experiments, which belong to Chapter 11.
Full modern quantum-mechanical orbital theory and probability distributions beyond the chapter’s brief limitations discussion.

known_pitfalls.claim: Most alpha particles were strongly deflected because atoms are mostly dense matter.
known_pitfalls.correction: Most alpha particles passed through because the atom is mostly empty space; only close encounters with the tiny nucleus produced large deflections.

known_pitfalls.claim: The Rutherford model explains atomic stability and line spectra.
known_pitfalls.correction: Classical electrodynamics predicts that its accelerating electron should radiate, spiral into the nucleus and emit a continuous spectrum.

known_pitfalls.claim: In Bohr’s model an electron radiates continuously while moving in an allowed orbit.
known_pitfalls.correction: A stationary orbit is non-radiating; radiation is emitted or absorbed only during a transition between allowed energy states.

known_pitfalls.claim: Bohr’s model works for all atoms.
known_pitfalls.correction: It successfully predicts gross features of hydrogenic single-electron atoms but cannot be extended successfully even to helium or explain relative spectral-line intensities.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with NCERT Example 12.1 to compare the empty-space proportions of an atom and the solar system.
Use NCERT Example 12.2 to calculate the distance of closest approach in alpha-particle scattering.
Use NCERT Example 12.3 to calculate hydrogen’s orbital radius and electron speed from the binding energy.
Apply NCERT Exercises 12.3 to 12.7 to transitions, kinetic and potential energies, photon wavelength, orbital speeds and radii.
Finish with NCERT Exercise 12.8 and the de Broglie standing-wave argument to connect energy levels with the hydrogen spectrum.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The end-of-chapter EXERCISES are numbered 12.1 to 12.9 and cover atomic models, scattering, energy-level transitions, Bohr radii and speeds, hydrogen wavelengths and angular-momentum quantisation.
